sections.text:
Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls.

Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections.

To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call.

Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples.

PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution.

Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.

summary.en: The paper introduces PICES, a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and its execution horizon by comparing nominal actions with their counterparts generated from perturbed noise samples. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks report up to 2.3× faster wall-clock policy inference on Jetson Orin and Thor than fixed-horizon baselines, along with improved success rates.
summary.zh: 论文提出免训练方法 PICES，在每次策略调用中根据名义动作块与扰动对应动作的差异，联合选择待执行动作块和再次调用策略前的执行步数。作者在仿真基准和真实操作任务中报告，相比固定执行视野基线，该方法在 Jetson Orin 和 Thor 上将策略推理墙钟时间最多加速 2.3 倍，同时提高成功率。

sections.text:
Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot.

Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers.

The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations.

In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error).

Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.

summary.en: The paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for a quadruped robot manipulating stacks of objects. Explicit base-height control enables three-dimensional pushing, with a high-level manipulation policy and a low-level locomotion policy. In simulation benchmarks, the authors report 90.3% success for single-object reposing and up to 90.1% for dynamic two-box stacks under strict position and orientation error limits. They also report zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 across payload masses and geometries.
summary.zh: 论文提出 SOMA，一种用于四足机器人操控多物体堆叠物的分层强化学习框架。它通过显式控制机器人底座高度实现三维推推，并将控制分为高层操控策略与低层运动策略。在仿真基准中，作者报告单物体重摆成功率为 90.3%，动态双箱堆叠最高为 90.1%，评估采用严格的位置和朝向误差界限。论文还报告，该方法在 Unitree Go1 上实现零样本仿真到现实迁移，并在不同载荷质量和几何形状下展示推挤过程中的底座高度调整。

sections.text:
Smartphones have become integral to modern life due to their diverse applications.

However, the development of applications for these devices faces significant challenges, primarily due to two factors: (i) the diverse hardware and operating system versions that require testing across multiple configurations; and (ii) the imperative activity of testing the smartphone in a non-invasive way (similar to an end-user interaction), which is expensive, tedious and error-prone as it is usually carried out manually.

In this context, robotic automation has emerged as an effective solution for addressing the diversity of smartphone systems and versions, and in performing some testing tasks non-invasively.

In addition, automated robots facilitate quick, accurate, and repetitive testing, thus enabling developers to validate their applications across various configurations effectively. This results in a less invasive verification and in a significant reduction in time spent on manual testing, thus accelerating the development cycle.

Our work proposes R-DLD (Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection), a robot-assisted infrastructure for data loss detection in Android applications, offeringless invasive and more realistic tests by interacting directly with smartphone sensors. The robot is constructed using cost-effective materials, facilitating its adoption in testing environments.

In our empirical evaluation R-DLD successfully identified 341 data loss issues in 77 randomly selected apps from an Android store. All reported bugs received responses from the developer, with 89.55% confirming the data loss problems, while 35.82% have being subsequently fixed.

summary.en: The paper proposes R-DLD, a robot-assisted infrastructure for detecting data loss in Android applications. It interacts directly with smartphone sensors to provide less invasive tests intended to resemble end-user interactions, and the robot is built from low-cost materials. In an empirical evaluation of 77 randomly selected apps from an Android store, R-DLD identified 341 data loss issues. Developers responded to all reported bugs; 89.55% confirmed the data loss, and 35.82% were subsequently fixed.
summary.zh: 论文提出 R-DLD，一种通过机器人直接与智能手机传感器交互、检测 Android 应用数据丢失的测试基础设施，旨在提供较少侵入且更贴近真实使用的测试。作者称该机器人采用低成本材料。在对应用商店随机选取的 77 款应用进行实证评估时，R-DLD 识别出 341 个数据丢失问题；所有报告的问题都收到开发者回应，其中 89.55% 获确认存在数据丢失，35.82% 随后得到修复。

items.title: Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection in Android Applications

sections.text:
Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others.

Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot.

Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering.

We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features.

In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.

summary.en: The paper addresses reward learning when human teaching underspecifies some task features. It shifts clarification work to the robot by using an informed prior to direct preference queries toward poorly supervised features and providing explanations to focus the human's attention. In simulation, the prior outperforms a standard active preference learning baseline by up to 30.8% in the low-query regime. A user study finds that the prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify one another.
summary.zh: 论文关注奖励学习中人类示教未能充分覆盖任务特征的问题，并提出由机器人承担后续澄清工作。方法利用示教数据识别监督不足的特征，以知情先验将偏好查询指向这些特征，并为每个查询附上引导人类注意相关特征的解释。在仿真中，该先验在低查询量条件下比标准主动偏好学习基线最高提升 30.8%。用户研究显示，知情先验和解释分别显著改善奖励恢复，二者结合时效果相互增强。

items.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards

sections.text:
Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstra- tions, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains chal- lenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand- crafted geometric mappings.

However, such mappings require meticulous recal- ibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines.

To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from ego- centric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human- action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decou- ples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters.

Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evalu- ation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.

summary.en: The paper presents EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns dexterous manipulation priors from egocentric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting. It learns effect-aware latent actions, models latent actions jointly with future visual dynamics, and adapts the model to robot embodiments through lightweight action adapters. In five real-world tasks across three embodiments, the authors report a 74% average success rate in out-of-domain evaluation versus 65% for a retargeting baseline, and a 47.2% reduction in cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost.
summary.zh: 论文提出 EgoJEPA，一种从第一人称人类视频学习灵巧操作先验的三阶段框架，旨在避免依赖手工的人到机器人动作重定向。框架先学习效果感知的潜在动作，再联合建模潜在动作与未来视觉动态，最后通过轻量动作适配器适配不同机器人。作者报告其在三种机器人本体的五项真实操作任务中，域外评估平均成功率为74%，重定向基线为65%；跨本体累计耗时降低47.2%。

items.title: EgoJEPA: Beyond Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Videos

sections.text:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) systems are fundamentally constrained by partial observability, as an agent can only accumulate knowledge from locations it has personally visited. As multiple robots increasingly coexist in shared environments, a natural question arises: can agents navigating the same space benefit from each other's observations?

In this work, we introduce Co-VLN, a minimalist, model-agnostic framework for systematically investigating whether and how peer observations from concurrently navigating agents can benefit VLN.

When independently navigating agents identify common traversed locations, they exchange structured perceptual memory, effectively expanding each agent's receptive field at no additional exploration cost.

We validate our framework on the R2R benchmark under two representative paradigms (the learning-based DUET and the zero-shot MapGPT), and conduct extensive analytical experiments to systematically reveal the underlying dynamics of peer observation sharing in VLN.

Results demonstrate that vision-sharing enabled model yields substantial performance improvements across both paradigms, establishing a strong foundation for future research in collaborative embodied navigation.

summary.en: The paper introduces Co-VLN, a model-agnostic framework for studying whether agents performing vision-language navigation can benefit from peer observations. When agents identify locations they have both traversed, they exchange structured perceptual memory, expanding each agent’s receptive field without additional exploration. The authors evaluate the approach on the R2R benchmark with the learning-based DUET and zero-shot MapGPT paradigms. They report substantial performance improvements with vision sharing across both paradigms, but the abstract gives no specific metrics or improvement sizes.
summary.zh: 论文研究在视觉语言导航中共享同一环境内其他导航智能体的观察是否有益，并提出模型无关框架 Co-VLN。智能体发现共同经过的位置后交换结构化感知记忆，以扩展彼此的感知范围，而不增加探索成本。作者在 R2R 基准上测试学习式 DUET 和零样本 MapGPT 两种范式，并报告视觉共享带来了显著性能提升。摘要未提供提升幅度或具体指标。

items.title: Does Peer Observation Help? Vision-Sharing Collaboration for Vision-Language Navigation

sections.text:
Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference.

We present TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing goals in the current motion.

A language model learns to predict support, root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision; their time-aligned encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator. Gravity-referenced states and trajectory--contact objectives improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body--time scopes and source-relative goals.

A separate reference-conditioned diffusion editor uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling-time projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality over the compared methods.

Controlled ablations support the value of motion-grounded conditioning and kinematic consistency, while multi-turn editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive relative requests under shared preservation constraints.

Together, these results support typed kinematic structure as a common basis for motion generation and reference-aware revision.

summary.en: The paper presents TRACE, a language-conditioned motion generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid. It grounds generation in typed support, root, and hand events derived from motion supervision, and uses gravity-referenced states and trajectory-contact objectives to improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests specify body-time scopes and goals relative to a reference motion; a separate diffusion editor applies changes while preserving protected state coordinates. The authors report better semantic alignment and motion quality than compared methods, and more reliable successive edits in multi-turn evaluations.
summary.zh: 论文提出 TRACE，用于 Unitree G1 人形机器人的语言条件动作生成与参考动作编辑。框架以可测量的支撑、根部和手部运动事件为条件，并利用动作监督、重力参考状态及轨迹接触目标改善运动一致性；编辑时，类型化请求指定身体部位、时间范围和相对当前动作的目标，参考条件扩散编辑器据此修改，同时保护指定状态。作者报告定量评估和人工评估优于对比方法，多轮编辑也更可靠；摘要未说明评估是否基于真实机器人实验。

items.title: TRACE: Typed Reference-Aware Conversational Editing for Humanoid Motion Diffusion

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success.

We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success.

To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

summary.en: The paper examines whether vision-language-action models follow How-level instructions that specify how to perform a task, rather than only what task to perform. The authors find that such instructions do not help current models and reduce task success. Enriching training with segment-level instructions makes actions responsive to them, but does not consistently increase success. The paper introduces SIMPLER-IN, which requires success conditions to be specified only in the instruction. Results indicate that responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions, leaving this an open challenge.
summary.zh: 论文考察视觉语言动作模型能否遵循说明执行任务的具体方式（How-level 指令），而不只是理解任务目标。作者发现，现有模型中的此类指令未带来帮助，反而降低任务成功率；按片段提供丰富指令可使动作对指令作出响应，但不能稳定提高成功率。论文提出 SIMPLER-IN，要求成功条件仅由指令给出。该评测显示，响应能力未能延伸至要求较高或分布外的指令，因此这类指令遵循仍是开放挑战。

sections.text:
Enabling robots to explore and act in unfamiliar environments under ambiguous human instructions by interactively identifying task-relevant objects (e.g., cups or beverages for "I'm thirsty") remains challenging for existing vision-language model (VLM)-based methods, due to inefficient reasoning and limited environmental interaction.

These factors hinder real-time task planning and execution.

To address this, we propose Affordance-Aware Interactive Decision-Making and Execution for Ambiguous Instructions (AIDE), a human-inspired dual-stream framework that integrates interactive exploration with vision-language reasoning: mirroring the complementary deliberative and intuitive processes of human cognition, Multi-Stage Inference (MSI) serves as the decision-making stream and Accelerated Decision-Making (ADM) as the execution stream, enabling zero-shot affordance analysis and interpretation of ambiguous instructions.

Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show that AIDE achieves over 80% task planning success rate and more than 95% closed-loop continuous execution accuracy at 10 Hz, surpassing existing VLM-based methods in diverse open scenarios.

summary.en: The paper proposes AIDE, a dual-stream framework for robot decision-making and execution under ambiguous instructions. It combines interactive exploration with vision-language reasoning, using Multi-Stage Inference for decisions and Accelerated Decision-Making for execution, with the stated aim of zero-shot affordance analysis. The authors report results from simulation and real-world experiments: task-planning success exceeded 80%, and closed-loop continuous execution accuracy exceeded 95% at 10 Hz. They also report that AIDE surpassed existing VLM-based methods in diverse open scenarios.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AIDE，一种面向模糊指令的双流机器人决策与执行框架，将多阶段推理用于决策，将加速决策用于执行，并结合交互式探索与视觉语言推理，以分析零样本可供性并解释指令。作者报告，仿真和真实环境实验中，该方法的任务规划成功率超过 80%，10 Hz 闭环连续执行准确率超过 95%，并称其在多种开放场景中优于已有视觉语言模型方法。

sections.text:
Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable.

This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model.

Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation.

An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF).

An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions.

Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.

summary.en: The paper presents a visual safety-certification method based on monocular optical flow. It represents collision risk through scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion, without reconstructing obstacle states or a metric world model. An online observer estimates normalized relative velocity and bounds its error; the framework propagates uncertainty into collision-cone constraints and uses a control-barrier-function program to adjust nominal control. The authors report simulation and TurtleBot3 real-world experiments with static and dynamic obstacles. The error bound contained measured error in 98.3% of simulation samples, and 93 of 100 real-world trials were collision-free.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种基于单目光流的视觉安全认证方法，以尺度无关、深度归一化的相对运动表示碰撞风险，无需重建障碍物状态或度量世界模型。框架通过在线观测器估计归一化相对速度并给出误差界，将不确定性纳入碰撞锥约束，再由控制障碍函数优化控制输入。作者报告，仿真与 TurtleBot3 真实实验展示了静态和动态障碍环境中的避碰；误差界覆盖 98.3% 的仿真测量误差，真实试验中 100 次有 93 次无碰撞导航。

items.title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion

sections.text:
Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction.

We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents.

LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts.

We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks.

Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable.

Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality.

We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse.

Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity.

Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points.

A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle.

Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.

Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso.

We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects.

Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry.

We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it.

The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff.

Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs.

To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior.

This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%.We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects

sections.text:
Vision-language-action models benefit from the understanding and reasoning capabilities of pretrained vision-language models, but action-only supervision provides limited grounding in world dynamics.

Conversely, world-action models inherit spatiotemporal priors from video generation models, yet remain limited in semantic understanding and reasoning under distribution shifts.

We introduce UniWAM, a unified architecture that integrates a physical reasoner, a world generator, and an action predictor to jointly learn semantic understanding of the physical world, visual generation, and action prediction.

To ensure the quality of the training data, we developed a rigorous data cleaning and annotation pipeline for both human egocentric data and robot data.

To adapt the vision-language component to embodied tasks while preserving its inherited language capabilities, we represent low-level actions in natural language and introduce a pre-training recipe that assigns complementary supervision from visual question answering (VQA) data, human egocentric data, and robot demonstrations to the appropriate model components.

During post-training, future visual noise augmentation reduces reliance on precise future predictions, while history-conditioned flow matching uses encoded action history to initialize action generation. Together, these designs significantly reduce denoising steps while maintaining performance.

UniWAM achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across multiple evaluations, including in-distribution performance, robustness, generalization, instruction following, and long-horizon task execution.

Furthermore, we uncover a log-linear scaling law of unified human-robot co-training, demonstrating the effectiveness of large-scale pre-training on a mixture of human and robot data.

summary.en: UniWAM combines a physical reasoner, world generator, and action predictor to jointly learn physical-world semantics, visual generation, and action prediction. The authors describe a data-cleaning and annotation pipeline for human egocentric and robot data, natural-language representations of low-level actions, and complementary pretraining supervision from VQA, human data, and robot demonstrations. Post-training uses future-visual-noise augmentation and history-conditioned flow matching. The authors report state-of-the-art results across several evaluations and a log-linear scaling law for unified human-robot co-training.

sections.text:
Bird's-eye-view (BEV) images have been demonstrated to provide valuable prior information for navigation. Given the global information provided by such views, two key challenges remain: how to fully exploit this information and how to reliably use it during execution.

In this paper, we propose a navigation system that uses BEV images as global priors and is designed for ground and near-ground robotic platforms. The system employs an image generation model to interpret human intent from natural language, identify the target destination, and generate traversability masks.

During execution, we introduce cross-view localization to align the robot's odometry with the BEV map and mitigate long-term drift in conventional odometry. We conduct extensive benchmark experiments to evaluate the proposed method and further validate its effectiveness on both UAV and quadruped robot platforms.

Using only a conventional local motion planner, the quadruped robot successfully completes a 285-meter outdoor long-range navigation task.

This work demonstrates how the world-understanding capabilities of foundation models can be transferred to embodied navigation, enabling robots to benefit from the strong generalization ability of existing image generation models.

summary.en: PathPainter proposes a navigation system for ground and near-ground robots that uses bird's-eye-view images as global priors. An image generation model interprets natural-language intent, identifies a destination, and generates traversability masks. During execution, cross-view localization aligns robot odometry with the BEV map to mitigate long-term drift. The authors report benchmark experiments and validation on UAV and quadruped platforms. In one reported task, a quadruped completed a 285-meter outdoor navigation route using only a conventional local motion planner.

sections.text:
Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments.

Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs.

To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module.

It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I2C, SPI, UART).Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions.

The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA).Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise.

By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.

summary.en: The paper introduces PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play black-box pedestrian dead-reckoning module for wearable and IoT platforms. It integrates a microprocessor and inertial measurement unit, performs real-time onboard sensor fusion, and provides position updates through I2C, SPI, or UART. Experimental evaluations report a step-detection error of 0.16% over 1,250 steps and a traveled-distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions, alongside 2.5 ms latency and 52.35 mA current consumption. The authors describe hardware-software co-design intended to ease integration and identify accuracy, power, and size improvements as future work.

Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch.

An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve.

Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs.

A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking.

During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%.These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.

summary.en: The paper presents a control barrier function allocator for maintaining desired wrench feasibility in tilting aerial robots under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. It reduces robust containment to thrust-margin constraints and a servo-rate optimization, and gives a conditional forward-invariance result. In MuJoCo studies of circular and cartwheel maneuvers, the method had lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During disturbed cartwheel rotation, the desired wrench was feasible at 1,751 stored samples; validating the nominal-trajectory certificate still requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.

Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons.

We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons.

Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement.

Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks.

SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.

summary.en: SPEAR is a framework for using vision-language models as preference oracles in robotic manipulation. It selects informative, distinguishable comparisons to reduce abstention, then uses an adaptive reward transition that begins with model-synthesized guidance before preference refinement. On manipulation benchmarks, the authors report 88.9% average success, 23.3 percentage points above baselines, with reduced abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. They also report fully online learning of three Mobile ALOHA tasks on real hardware.

Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence.

We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS.

A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints.

Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.

summary.en: The paper proposes a symbolic supervisory control architecture for motion learned from demonstrations. It automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan and certifies safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility from robot dynamics, independently of the learned dynamical system. A nominal controller tracks the learned motion while a supervisor monitors safety and goal convergence and intervenes when needed. The authors report simulations and real-robot deployments across varied two- and three-dimensional datasets, including handwriting, as evidence of effectiveness in providing formal guarantees in complex, dynamic environments.

sections.text:
Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable.

Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it must first learn to play. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to play matter for precise assembly?

We propose Play2Perfect, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals, which is then perfected on precise assembly. The goal of play is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching.

Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in play pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision.

We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.

summary.en: Play2Perfect is an RL framework that pretrains multi-fingered robots through task-agnostic play with diverse objects and goals, then fine-tunes the resulting manipulation priors for precise assembly. The authors study object diversity, training objectives, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. They report that the learned prior is 33 times more sample-efficient than training RL from scratch, even with dense multi-stage rewards. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, it achieves 60% success on tight insertions with 0.5 mm contact clearance and over 50% on long-horizon multipart assembly and screwing.

sections.text:
Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users.

We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training.

Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information.

Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission.

Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability.

Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

summary.en: AVALON targets indoor settings familiar to people but unseen by the robot, without prior site traversal or site-specific training. It combines human-seeded layered topological memory, node-verified execution, and task-triggered memory updates gated by field evidence. Deployment uses a floor plan, place clues, and initial topology-odometry alignment; verified arrivals support re-anchoring without a robot-built global SLAM map. Humans provide visually unobservable constraints and report environmental changes, while the robot validates physical conditions. In Unitree Go2 experiments, AVALON with X-NavDP completed a 12.81 m mission in 46.4 seconds in all five runs; the abstract reports 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2, while policy-only X-NavDP timed out in all five runs.
summary.zh: AVALON面向用户熟悉、机器人未曾到访且没有现场训练的室内环境，结合人工提供的分层拓扑记忆、节点验证执行，以及按任务触发并受证据约束的人机记忆更新。系统以平面图、地点线索和初始拓扑里程计对齐为部署条件，通过已验证节点重新锚定位置，无需机器人构建全局SLAM地图。人类提供视觉无法观察的任务约束和环境变化信息，机器人通过现场验证提供物理状态证据。Unitree Go2实验中，AVALON与X-NavDP完成12.81米任务的5次运行均成功，耗时46.4秒；摘要报告其比DimOS-Go2少用40.9%机器人时间，而单独使用X-NavDP的5次运行均超时。

sections.text:
Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment.

For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories.

Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories.

Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50.

Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50.Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences.

These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

summary.en: The paper proposes two-level on-policy distillation for flow-based vision-language-action models, addressing distribution mismatch in both environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. Multiple frozen domain specialists supervise one student, which gathers fresh environment experience and generates new action-flow trajectories after each update; teachers provide velocity supervision along those trajectories. From a joint supervised fine-tuning initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. The authors also report gains over two comparison methods across the benchmarks and larger improvements on longer CALVIN sequences.
summary.zh: 本文提出面向流式视觉语言动作模型的两级在线策略蒸馏方法，以缓解学生策略部署时环境观测和动作生成中间状态的分布差异。多个冻结的领域专家共同指导一个学生策略；学生每次更新后与环境交互并生成新的动作流轨迹，教师沿这些轨迹提供速度监督。以联合监督微调为起点，速度损失蒸馏在LIBERO-40、CALVIN五指令序列和Meta-World MT50上分别带来22.55%、33.4%和22.6%的成功率绝对增益。作者还报告，该方法相较动作损失蒸馏和教师轨迹监督微调在三个基准上均有额外增益，且CALVIN较长序列的提升更大。

sections.text:
Contact-rich robotic tasks require coordinated motion and impedance under uncertain interaction dynamics and physical constraints. While recent methods on learned policies provide useful interaction strategies, they may fail when contact conditions differ from those encountered during training.

Model-based generative methods show promising receding-horizon trajectories optimization results, but often lack structured behavioral guidance and refinement that jointly accounts for constraint geometry and actual contact responses.

To this end, we propose Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion--impedance optimization. MGA first organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into structured sequence proposals, retaining task-specific interaction strategies without committing to their execution.

It then evaluates these proposals alongside exploratory samples through model-based rollouts for refinement or separate execution selection.

Crucially, realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates from the refinement bank with both task constraints and locally achievable physical responses, allowing learned experience to guide online adaptation under changing contact conditions.

Experiments cover surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved safety success rate of impedance control under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.

summary.en: The paper presents Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion and impedance optimization in contact-rich tasks with uncertain interactions and physical constraints. MGA organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into sequence proposals that retain task-specific strategies without committing to execution. Model-based rollouts evaluate these proposals alongside exploratory samples for refinement or separate execution selection. Its realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates with task constraints and locally achievable physical responses to support online adaptation as contact conditions change. The abstract reports improved safety success rates for impedance control in surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing experiments under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.
summary.zh: 本文提出流形生成退火（MGA），一种结合无模型与基于模型生成方法的运动和阻抗联合优化框架，面向接触条件不确定且受物理约束的机器人任务。MGA先将预训练强化学习策略组织成序列提案，以保留任务相关交互策略，但不直接执行；随后通过基于模型的推演评估提案和探索样本，用于细化或单独选择执行方案。其实现感知的流形细化使更新同时考虑任务约束和局部可实现的物理响应，以支持接触条件变化时的在线适应。摘要称，表面扫描、插销插入和人形机器人推推动作实验中，阻抗控制在名义条件及感知偏移条件下的安全成功率有所提高。

sections.text:
Safe whole-body control requires coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics--making safety certificates difficult to design and reuse across behaviors. We present LIMBO, a framework for synthesizing a state-action control barrier function and distilling its safety structure into a task policy.

LIMBO learns the safety certificate from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification over residual actions around a frozen base controller, making Q-CBF synthesis tractable in the full control dimension while placing the certificate in the task policy's control space.

During synthesis, the learned safety value drives risk-guided sampling near the estimated boundary of recoverability; during task learning, it serves as a teacher that provides action-level safety feedback, yielding a robust task policy and alleviating the need for an online safety filter at deployment.

We demonstrate LIMBO on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. Beyond scaling learned Q-CBFs to whole-body control, we show that risk-guided boundary sampling provides a theoretically grounded way to explore the edge of recoverability.

Under the same safety specification, ceteris paribus, varying the sampling concentration produces strategies ranging from crouching to a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver. In both settings, the learned policies transfer to hardware without online safety filtering, showing that learned safety synthesis scales to agile whole-body control.

summary.en: LIMBO learns a control barrier function from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification, then distills its safety structure into a task policy. Risk-guided sampling explores the estimated recoverability boundary, while the learned value gives action-level safety feedback during task learning. The authors demonstrate the approach with a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid in dodgeball-avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion tasks, and report hardware transfer without online safety filtering. They also report that changing sampling concentration yields different strategies, including crouching and backward leaning.
summary.zh: LIMBO 从黑箱状态转移和基于状态的失败规范中学习控制障碍函数，并将安全结构蒸馏进任务策略。它通过风险引导采样探索可恢复边界，并在任务学习中提供动作级安全反馈。作者在29自由度人形机器人仿真任务及硬件上展示了躲避躲避球、低障碍下行走等行为；硬件迁移无需在线安全过滤。作者还称，改变采样集中程度可在下蹲与后仰穿越等策略间产生变化。

items.title: LIMBO: Learning and Internalizing Model-Free Barrier Objectives for Agile and Safe Whole-Body Control

sections.text:
Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance.

However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions.

This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution.

The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs.

Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4s to 24.4s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m.

It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.

summary.en: CLIS-MPPI addresses the mismatch between simulated and actual states caused by planning delay. It models delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, optimizes rollouts from sampled states, and applies a rollout-based local feedback correction during execution. In real-world narrow-passage experiments with a UR5e manipulator, CLIS-MPPI had no collisions in five runs, while standard MPPI collided in two. Across each method’s collision-free runs, the authors report lower completion time, end-effector path length, and joint-position and joint-velocity errors for CLIS-MPPI.
summary.zh: CLIS-MPPI 针对规划延迟导致的仿真状态与执行时实际状态不一致，将延迟建模为可能执行初始状态的分布，从采样状态进行轨迹优化，并在执行时加入基于轨迹的局部反馈修正。作者在 UR5e 机械臂窄通道避障与目标到达任务中进行了真实实验：5次运行中，该方法均未碰撞，而标准 MPPI 有2次碰撞。作者还报告，按各自无碰撞运行计算，CLIS-MPPI 的完成时间、路径长度及关节位置和速度误差均较低。

items.title: CLIS-MPPI: Closed-Loop Model Predictive Path Integral Control With Initial-State Sampling Under Execution Delay

sections.text:
Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them.

We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress.

The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them.

We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement.

Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget.

On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

summary.en: CoDA co-evolves a simulation data engine and an action policy through shared memory containing environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. Validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic are compiled into programs for recreating difficulties and training programs for overcoming them. Its Text2potential method turns diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning. Across four manipulation task families, the authors report out-of-distribution success rising from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%. On LIBERO-Pro, after 15 rounds, success reaches 84% under position perturbations and 76% under instruction perturbations.
summary.zh: CoDA 让仿真数据引擎与动作策略通过共享异构记忆共同演进。记忆将视觉语言批评器验证过的诊断转化为重现困难的环境生成程序，以及帮助策略克服困难的训练程序。作者提出 Text2potential，将诊断转为分阶段势函数，为动作片段价值学习提供密集监督；学习进展则指导后续生成与程序调整。在四类操作任务中，作者报告分布外成功率由监督微调后的5.3%升至27.6%；在 LIBERO-Pro 上，经过15轮后，位置扰动和指令扰动下的成功率分别达到84%和76%。

items.title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

sections.text:
Design for Robotic Assembly (DfRA) remains largely dependent on manual planning and heuristic simulation, limiting scalability and robustness in complex industrial settings.

Although large language models (LLMs) show promise for semantic reasoning and task planning, most approaches remain tightly coupled to pre-built simulators that assume an accurate world model.

We introduce Iterative Design for Robotic Assembly (IDfRA), a closed-loop framework that combines an LLM for plan generation with a vision-language model (VLM) for execution assessment.

Given a target structure and a partial environmental signature, the LLM proposes an assembly plan, the robot executes it once at test time, and the VLM evaluates the resulting state to provide feedback for replanning. Through this iterative planning-execution-verification loop, the system progressively improves semantic fidelity and physical feasibility.

Crucially, IDfRA does not require an accurate a priori world model before deployment. Instead, physical constraints are discovered online through interaction, enabling adaptation to under-specified environments. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that IDfRA attains 73.3% top-1 accuracy in semantic recognisability, surpassing the baseline on this metric.

Moreover, the resulting assembly plans exhibit robust physical feasibility, achieving an overall 86.9% construction success rate, with design quality improving across iterations, albeit not always monotonically. Pairwise human evaluation further corroborates the advantages of IDfRA relative to alternative approaches.

By integrating self-verification with context-aware adaptation, the framework evidences strong potential for deployment in unstructured manufacturing scenarios.

summary.en: IDfRA combines large-language-model plan generation with vision-language-model assessment of assembly outcomes. Given a target structure and partial environmental information, the robot executes a plan, the model evaluates the result, and feedback supports replanning. The framework discovers physical constraints through interaction and does not require an accurate prior world model before deployment. In empirical evaluation, the authors report 73.3% top-1 accuracy in semantic recognisability and an overall construction success rate of 86.9%. Design quality improves across iterations, though not monotonically, and pairwise human evaluations also support advantages over alternatives.
summary.zh: IDfRA 将大语言模型的装配计划生成与视觉语言模型的执行评估结合起来：机器人依据目标结构和部分环境信息执行计划，视觉语言模型评估结果并反馈以便重新规划。该闭环通过交互在线发现物理约束，不要求部署前具备准确的先验世界模型。经验评估中，作者报告语义可识别性 top-1 准确率为73.3%，总体建造成功率为86.9%；设计质量随迭代改善，但并非总是单调上升。成对人工评估也支持其相对优势。

items.title: IDfRA: Self-Verification for Iterative Design in Robotic Assembly

sections.text:
Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact.

We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched.

Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization.

Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map.

It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/

summary.en: The paper proposes a training-free refinement method for distilled 3D Gaussian language maps. A text-promptable segmenter identifies target regions, whose visual embeddings are blended with target text embeddings; other regions remain unchanged. The method derives the smallest coefficient that lets each target win in closed form and uses centering at readout to address query-agnostic behavior caused by shared components in text embeddings. The authors report improvements across three benchmarks, roughly doubled base mIoU on Replica, better language-goal localization, plug-in transfer to existing maps, and a legged-robot demonstration.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种无需训练的目标感知细化方法，在已蒸馏的3D高斯语言地图中，借助可由文本提示的分割器，将检测目标区域的视觉嵌入与目标文本嵌入按凸组合融合，并保持非目标区域不变。方法为每个目标以闭式解求取仍能使其胜出的最小融合系数，并通过读出阶段的中心化缓解文本嵌入共有成分导致的查询无关问题。作者报告，该方法在三个基准上改善开放词汇分割，在Replica上使基础mIoU约翻倍，并提升语言目标定位；还展示了其对现成语言地图的迁移及四足机器人导航演示。

sections.text:
Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We present Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) model that uses touch in two complementary ways.

During pretraining, image-space contact maps derived from tactile gloves, together with features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher, supervise the visual tokens; these objectives are removed at inference. In parallel, a tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states to condition the action expert.

A single checkpoint therefore supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment. To scale this supervision, we build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and pretrain Spark-0 on it together with egocentric video, robot data, and simulation.

We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Spark-0 achieves the highest mean success rate on both SparkArena tracks and ranks first on all eight aggregate metrics of the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark.

Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining.

The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.

summary.en: The paper presents Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action model. During pretraining, image-space contact maps from tactile gloves and features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher supervise visual tokens; a separate tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states for the action expert. The same checkpoint supports vision-only or tactile-conditioned deployment. The authors build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and report top results on SparkArena and all eight aggregate Ego Humanoid metrics. Comparisons also show gains when tactile data is retained during pretraining.

sections.text:
Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map.

We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.

Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema.

The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions.

The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path.

In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%.

The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.

summary.en: The paper presents a modular, fully onboard UAV navigation pipeline that converts visual observations into obstacle-specific safety constraints. A shared BLIP encoder supports captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, fused with depth for 3D localization. A lightweight LLM infers category risks using retrieval-augmented generation and constrained decoding; verdicts are cached by category, and obstacle identities persist through occlusions. On a Jetson Orin NX, perception runs at 10 Hz, while fallback LLM queries take about 0.8 seconds outside the control-critical path. In Gazebo, the authors report fewer collisions than a geometric planner and higher success for semantics-aware landing among moving actors. The abstract notes limits on small-object perception at range.

sections.text:
When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable.

We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games).Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario.

Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality.

To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information.

We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases.

These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

summary.en: The paper presents a multi-agent motion-planning framework based on games with partially ordered preferences, deriving scenario-specific preferences and games from general legal guidelines. The authors prove that refining agent preferences or updating guidelines can only remove equilibria, preserving legality, and introduce coordination methods that avoid explicit disclosure of private preferences. In seven maritime encounters involving up to four vessels, they report that every violation in committed equilibria was certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors were identified from public information in all tested cases.

sections.text:
Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task.

Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints.

In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches.

Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints.

Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras.

Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app

summary.en: The paper proposes RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow-matching framework for estimating camera-to-robot pose from monocular images. It extracts keypoint positional and contextual features from 2D heatmaps, uses a learnable keypoint adjacency map to condition flow matching, and adds bone-length and ray-depth losses for topology consistency and scale stability. The authors report better pose-estimation performance than existing methods across robot types and cameras, and introduce a cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate zero-shot cross-scene performance.

sections.text:
Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance.

We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions.

Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task.

PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks.

Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5.

Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/

summary.en: The paper proposes a proactive-robot framework using Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM). A vision-language task predictor consults the memory and current observations to decide when and how to assist, while a vision-language-action executor performs the task. PAM represents activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection model revises it from daily interaction traces without weight updates or retraining. In a five-day desk-assistance evaluation, the authors report improving performance with experience, the highest precision, recall, and F1, and a first-fire delay declining from about five seconds on Day 1 to one second on Day 5.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种依靠程序化辅助记忆的主动机器人框架：视觉语言模型任务预测器结合当前观察和记忆决定何时提供帮助及执行何种任务，视觉语言动作执行器完成任务。记忆以活动阶段有限状态机、各状态辅助规则和事件驱动转移构成，并由反思模型根据每日交互记录修订，无需更新权重或重新训练。在为期五天的桌面辅助评估中，作者报告系统随经验积累持续提升，取得最高的精确率、召回率和 F1；首次触发延迟从第一天约五秒降至第五天一秒。

items.title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory

sections.text:
Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations. Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are specialized for a single task.

Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions.

In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates.

First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel.

We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates. Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour.

See our website for policy rollout videos: demostream.github.io.

summary.en: The paper presents DemoStream, a task-and-motion planning system designed to optimize demonstration quality and improve behavior-cloning success. It introduces batched TAMP sampling and a corresponding constraint-satisfaction algorithm to explore solutions in parallel. Simulation experiments examine how action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes affect downstream policy success. The authors also report collecting real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 per hour, using TAMP safety guarantees.
summary.zh: 论文提出 DemoStream，一种利用 GPU 加速任务与运动规划（TAMP）的系统，旨在优化演示质量并提升行为克隆成功率。方法包括批量 TAMP 采样和相应的批量约束满足算法，以并行探索多种解。仿真实验比较不同动作空间、代价函数和批量大小对下游策略成功率的影响；作者还报告利用 TAMP 的安全保证，在真实世界以平均每小时 66 条的速率收集演示。

items.title: DemoStream: Batched Task-and-Motion-Plan Optimization for Automated Learning from Demonstration
